wording (Hebrew sense): never inhabited for all generations; desolate forever; no stone taken from you
outcome: inhabited and important 539 BCE - 1st c. CE (Alexander died there 323; a Greek inscription of 166 BCE; cuneiform to 1st c. CE); deserted by 2nd c. CE; bricks quarried for later towns; villages on parts of the site in modern times
status: came true ~650 years after the conquest the text links it to; 'no stone taken' did not

wording (Hebrew sense): a desolation, dry as the desert, a lair for animals; no healing for your wound
outcome: destroyed 612; Xenophon (401 BCE) passed a huge deserted city he calls Mespila (identification with Nineveh is modern); a town of Ninos still existed in 49 CE (Tacitus); Mosul across the river
remained a major city through Persian, Ptolemaic and Roman times; declined after Alexandria and was abandoned after Fustat/Cairo (7th c. CE)
no such 40-year desolation; Amasis (570-526) ruled a prosperous Egypt

wording (Hebrew sense): you will never be rebuilt; you will be no more forever
outcome: rebuilt after 332; a large city in Roman times; largely ruined 1291-c.1800; a city today

wording (Hebrew sense): will cease to be a city, a heap of ruins
perpetual wastes; no one will live there; desolate from generation to generation
outcome: Nabataean kingdom flourished in Edom's land (Petra); Bozrah = Buseirah, an inhabited town
status: did not happen (land); the Edomites as a people did disappear

wording (Hebrew sense): cities desolate with no inhabitant; Moab like Sodom, perpetual waste
outcome: Moab's towns (Dibon, Madaba, Kir/Kerak) continued; the Moabites as a people disappeared

wording (Hebrew sense): Rabbah a pasture for camels; not remembered among the nations
status: did not happen (city); the Ammonites as a people disappeared

wording (Hebrew sense): Ashkelon will not be inhabited; a desolation
outcome: destroyed 604, rebuilt; major city until destroyed in 1270 CE

wording (Hebrew sense): a heap in the field, stones poured into the valley
outcome: rebuilt after 720; razed c.108 BCE; rebuilt as Sebaste; village today

wording (Hebrew sense): an everlasting waste, no one will live there
